scholar_renderings.renders: position, explicitly and self-consciously — she names the layer language as a spatial rendering: "we transform a genetic way of looking at a problem, as it were, into a spatial one" and calls the resulting topology a methodological help. Her diagram legends call each region a sphere, and elsewhere she writes of a layer of the personal overlying the collective unconscious.

items.boundary_rule_implicated: if the claim entails the subject is materially a constituent of the object → composition; if it locates the subject within the object's structure without asserting constituency → position
items.notes: The strongest single result in this worksheet: the source states the very distinction the boundary rule draws, and lands on the position side. It also supplies a caution the graph may want — Jacobi treats the spatial reading as a heuristic overlay on a genetic one, so an edge that records position is recording her methodological help, not a claim of the text.

items.score_reason: Jacobi's rendering supports correspondence and Edinger's supports identity for the same relation, so named sources land in different families.
items.boundary_rule_implicated: both CW 9ii §60 edges ... are `correspondence`. The test is what the text predicates indistinguishability OF, not what the nodes are
items.notes: JOINT FINDING FOR 26 AND 27, which is what the purposive pair was drawn to test. The literature does NOT recognize the sentence-subject distinction. Edinger discusses §60 directly and does not mark it off from any other mandala/God-image statement; his own equivalence claim at p. 36 makes no reference to whether the predication falls on the terms or on their symbols. Jacobi renders every mandala/God-image statement the same way — symbol and correspondence — regardless of grammatical subject. The split that the literature does show is a split between scholars (Jacobi vs Edinger), and it runs across both paragraphs identically rather than between them. So: the v0.6 sentence-subject test produces a difference the secondary literature does not make, and the two families it assigns to §572 and §60 correspond to two scholarly camps, not to two Jungian claims. That is a real external-validity finding and it cuts against the rule as a general instrument, though it does not show the individual assignments are wrong.
